prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The space shuttle Discovery is on pace for a Sunday launch after NASA engineers repaired a leaky gas venting system, officials said Saturday. Space shuttle Discovery readies for launch, which now appears on pace for Sunday. The leak had canceled a planned launch on Wednesday. NASA hopes the seven-member crew can take off around 7:40 p.m. Sunday on a mission to the international space station, where they will deliver supplies needed to expand the station's crew to six people. "The vehicle is looking real good ... ," lead shuttle flight director Mike Moses said. "Basically, I think I can sum this up by just saying we're good to go tomorrow and we're looking forward to getting the count going." A leak in a hydrogen gas vent line forced Wednesday's delay. Repairs went smoothly, Moses said. The line funnels flammable hydrogen away from the launch pad during takeoff. The shuttle crew will be delivering the final parts needed for an expanded solar energy power system that will allow the station to double its crew to six people. The crew also will be dropping off Japanese astronaut Koichi Wakata, who will replace NASA's Sandy Magnus on the space station. The shuttle also will carry a replacement for a failed unit in a system that converts urine to drinkable water, NASA said.  Watch an explanation of why Wednesday's launch was scrubbed » . Kathy Winters, the mission's chief weather officer, said Sunday appears to offer only a 20 percent chance of weather that would scrub the launch. The crew, led by commander Lee Archambault, is expected to board Discovery at Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral, Florida, at about 4:30 p.m. Sunday. Officials said the crew has been training and resting for the mission since Wednesday. Earlier this week, Magnus, station commander Michael Fincke and Russian engineer Yury Lonchakov had to take shelter in their Soyuz spacecraft -- a lifeboat of sorts -- when a piece of debris from an earlier mission hurtled uncomfortably close to the station. The debris, moving about 20,000 mph, came within three miles of the station but caused no damage. Wednesday's launch postponement was the latest in a series of delays for Discovery as it tries to make the 28th shuttle mission to the space station. The launch had been delayed previously to allow time to check a "flow-control valve in the shuttle's main engines," NASA said last week. That resulted from damage being found in a valve on the shuttle Endeavour during its November 2008 flight. Three valves were cleared and installed on Discovery, it said. CNN's Kim Segal and John Zarella contributed to this report.

(CNN) -- The space shuttle Discovery remains on track for a Sunday launch after NASA engineers repaired a leak in its gas-venting system, officials said Saturday.

The leak had forced NASA to cancel a planned launch on Wednesday. NASA now hopes the seven-member crew can lift off at about 7:40 p.m. Sunday on a mission to the International Space Station, where they will deliver supplies needed to expand the station’s crew to six people.

“The vehicle is looking real good ...,” said lead shuttle flight director Mike Moses. “Basically, I think I can sum this up by just saying we’re good to go tomorrow and we’re looking forward to getting the count going.”

The leak occurred in a hydrogen gas vent line, which carries flammable hydrogen away from the launch pad during takeoff. Repairs went smoothly, Moses said.

Discovery’s crew will deliver the final components needed for an expanded solar power system, which will allow the space station to double its crew to six people. The shuttle also will bring Japanese astronaut Koichi Wakata to the station. Wakata will replace NASA astronaut Sandy Magnus aboard the orbiting laboratory.

In addition, Discovery will carry a replacement for a failed unit in a system that converts urine into drinkable water, NASA said.

Kathy Winters, the mission’s chief weather officer, said conditions Sunday appear favorable, with only a 20 percent chance that weather would force another launch delay.

The crew, led by commander Lee Archambault, is expected to board Discovery at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida, at about 4:30 p.m. Sunday. Officials said the astronauts have been training and resting for the mission since Wednesday.

Earlier this week, Magnus, station commander Michael Fincke, and Russian engineer Yury Lonchakov had to take shelter in their Soyuz spacecraft — which serves as a lifeboat of sorts — when a piece of debris from an earlier mission passed uncomfortably close to the station. The debris, traveling at about 20,000 mph, came within three miles of the station but caused no damage.

Wednesday’s postponement was the latest in a series of delays for Discovery as it seeks to complete the 28th shuttle mission to the space station. The launch had previously been delayed to allow time to inspect a “flow-control valve in the shuttle’s main engines,” NASA said last week. That inspection followed the discovery of damage in a valve on the shuttle Endeavour during its November 2008 flight. Three valves were cleared and installed on Discovery, NASA said.

CNN’s Kim Segal and John Zarella contributed to this report.

The leak was found in the shuttle’s external fuel tank venting system, which safely routes excess hydrogen gas away from the launch pad during fueling. NASA officials said technicians completed repairs and inspections at Kennedy Space Center and were continuing final checks ahead of the countdown.

The issue had raised concerns because hydrogen is highly flammable, and even small leaks in the vent system can force a launch delay. Similar problems have interrupted shuttle launch attempts in the past.

Mission managers are expected to review weather, technical readiness and range safety conditions before giving final approval for launch.

*Discovery* is one of NASA’s most flown orbiters and has played a central role in assembly and servicing missions throughout the shuttle program. The upcoming flight is part of NASA’s continuing effort to support station operations and deliver key components before the shuttle fleet is retired.

**NASA Targets New Launch Attempt for Shuttle Discovery After Hydrogen Leak Scrub**

**CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. —** NASA is preparing for another attempt to launch space shuttle **Discovery** after a Wednesday countdown was halted by a potentially dangerous hydrogen gas leak, delaying a mission to deliver the final major set of solar power hardware to the International Space Station.

The launch had been scrubbed during fueling when sensors detected a leak in the system used to vent gaseous hydrogen from Discovery’s external tank. NASA engineers traced the problem to hardware near the **ground umbilical carrier plate**, where the external tank connects to a vent line that safely carries hydrogen away from the shuttle during tanking.

Hydrogen leaks are treated with extreme caution because the gas is highly flammable. NASA launch managers called off the attempt rather than risk continuing with the countdown.

Since the scrub, technicians have worked at the launch pad to repair the leak area, replacing seals and inspecting the connection that failed during fueling. NASA officials said the repairs were aimed at ensuring a tight seal when super-cold liquid hydrogen is loaded again into the shuttle’s external tank.

If testing and countdown preparations remain on track, NASA is targeting a new launch opportunity in the coming days. Weather is expected to be a factor, but forecasters have indicated generally favorable conditions, with the main concerns likely to include clouds, winds or possible showers near Kennedy Space Center.

Discovery’s mission, designated **STS-119**, is one of the final assembly flights for the International Space Station. Its primary goal is to deliver and install the station’s last major solar array segment, known as the **S6 truss**. Once installed and deployed, the new solar wings will expand the station’s electrical power capacity, supporting a larger crew and additional scientific research aboard the orbiting laboratory.

The shuttle crew is led by **Commander Lee Archambault**, with **Tony Antonelli** serving as pilot. Mission specialists include **Joseph Acaba**, **Richard Arnold**, **John Phillips**, **Steve Swanson**, and Japanese astronaut **Koichi Wakata**. Wakata is scheduled to remain aboard the station as a long-duration crew member, replacing astronaut **Sandra Magnus**, who is due to return to Earth aboard Discovery.

The mission includes multiple spacewalks to attach the new truss segment, connect power and data cables, and prepare the solar arrays for deployment. The work is considered a major milestone in completing the station’s backbone and power-generation system.

The delay comes during an eventful week for the station. The orbiting outpost’s current crew recently took precautionary shelter in a docked Russian **Soyuz** spacecraft after NASA was alerted to a piece of orbital debris passing close to the complex. The warning came too late to perform an avoidance maneuver, prompting the crew to temporarily move into the Soyuz, which serves as their emergency lifeboat. The debris passed without incident, and the crew later resumed normal operations.

NASA officials said the debris scare did not affect Discovery’s launch preparations, but it underscored the risks of operating in an increasingly crowded orbital environment.

Discovery’s flight is among the shuttle program’s remaining missions before retirement, adding urgency to NASA’s effort to complete station assembly. Launch managers said they will proceed only if the repaired venting system performs properly during fueling and weather conditions meet safety requirements.
